A Confucian accepts this, because the small daily acts of propriety are not overheads to be delegated but the practice through which a person is formed. Getting names right matters here. A birthday message an assistant chose and sent is not quite a son remembering his mother, and calling it that hides the fact that the remembering has stopped.

Ritual propriety is not etiquette for its own sake. It is the shared form through which people show each other what they mean to one another, and a gesture chosen by an assistant carries the form without the person who was supposed to be in it. A host lets an app plan the menu for her in-laws. The meal is better than she would have managed, and the evening carries nothing she chose for them.

A Utilitarian will object that if the present is better and the people involved are happier, the only cost is a sentiment about who did the choosing. But the choosing is not a sentiment; it is the conduct through which the relationship exists. A better present from no one in particular improves an object and weakens the tie it was meant to express. Conduct grows through practice inside one's relationships, so outsourcing the practice thins the relationships themselves.

Handing these choices over costs something, even when the assistant chooses better, because what you owe the people around you is shown in choosing for them yourself. Cultivating oneself proceeds through roles and ritual, not apart from them. Remembering a parent's preferences, choosing what to bring a host, deciding how to answer a colleague: these are the forms in which humaneness is practised, and practice is what forms it.

It costs something that matters. Conduct is learned by doing it within one's roles, and the daily choices made as a parent, a friend or a colleague are where a person becomes humane. Relationships constitute a person; you are somebody's child, somebody's friend. If the choices that make up those relationships are made elsewhere, the relationships thin out, and the person they were making thins out with them.

An Ubuntu Ethicist will object that the Confucian treats the relationship as a matter of role duties, when what matters is what the people become through each other, which a shared assistant need not damage. Roles are not the opposite of what people become through each other; they are the forms that becoming takes. The worry is exactly that the assistant removes the occasions on which people meet each other in those forms. Trading the practice of one's roles for better choices is a poor exchange.
